money_at_stake.rationale: This candidate record carries no full occurrence block (no `kind`, `window`, or `occurrence.anchor_date`; only a top-level `date`), consistent with method section 0.1: ambient candidates are pre-signal-bar and lighter-weight than promoted signal cards. I therefore appraise the pool this single political development is evidence of, not a number invented for the headline alone. The candidate's own thesis is that this Michigan Republican Senate candidate backing a moratorium matters mainly if the moratorium trend spreads across states. By 2026-08-30 that spread is no longer hypothetical: a dated national tracker (Data Center Watch, reported by Forbes) found data-center opponents blocked or delayed at least 75 projects worth about USD 130bn nationally in Q1 2026 alone, and two large states had already converted that backlash into live state action (New York's statewide hyperscale moratorium, Texas's grid-connection freeze pending an ERCOT audit of an interconnection queue that itself runs into the hundreds of gigawatts). GT_100B is supported by the USD 130bn single-quarter figure on its own, without needing to add the Michigan-specific or Texas-specific figures on top of it (deliberately not summed into one bigger headline number, matching the caution the reference SIG-20260829-01 appraisal used for its three national programs). The single Michigan project this moratorium would most directly threaten, the OpenAI/Oracle 'Barn' campus in Saline Township, is itself a cited USD 16bn investment, expected to be the largest data center in Michigan by both power capacity and physical size, which independently anchors a real Michigan-specific pool even before counting the national trend.

capture_odds.rationale: Genuinely two-sided and scored close to the middle rather than rounded toward either story. Against capture: this occurrence is itself regulatory risk in its purest form, a live example (New York's Executive Order No. 62, covering data centers of 50 megawatts or more) of a state converting political backlash into an actual construction freeze rather than a proposal, which is exactly the 'regulated away' failure mode the anchor table describes; a Michigan moratorium that passed after the 2026 elections would do the same to the state's own pipeline. For capture: as of this occurrence's own date, the listed equipment tier behind the buildout had not yet seen that risk convert into lost revenue. GE Vernova raised full-year 2026 guidance, reporting orders up 88% organically to USD 24.2bn and Gas Power equipment backlog and slot reservation agreements growing from 100 to 116 GW (expected to reach at least 125 GW by year-end 2026), in the same reporting window the moratorium wave was accelerating, and national demand that is blocked in one state (Texas, New York) is not obviously destroyed, since the same listed suppliers serve whichever state or country the capex relocates to. Scored on that evidence of resilience so far, not assumed away, which is why it sits below the reachable/opportunity threshold rather than at the regulated-return floor.
